World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Deaths of Pacific islander farm workers ripple through small country town
World.content:
Residents of a small West Australian town have come together to mourn the deaths of two Vanuatu farm workers as investigations into their deaths continue.

The two men died, and a third was critically injured, when their car crashed into a tree just south of Manjimup, 290 kilometres south of Perth.

The lower South West is popular for migrant workers, with almost 400 in the region brought to Australia through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme (PALM).

The ABC has been told the two men were no longer part of the scheme at the time of their death.

Two weeks on from the crash, the islander community is continuing to mourn the men and to raise money for their families.

Support being provided

A gathering for the region's PALM workers was held at the Manjimup Hotel last week, to provide support for the broader islander community.

Workers gathered in Manjimup to mourn the men this week. (Supplied)

David Cooper from labour hire company TeamsWork said the workers who died were not employed by his firm, but the tragedy had a broader impact.

"We employ a number of people from Vanuatu, along with other regions, and this has a rippling effect, not only through the Vanuatu community, but also through the other PALM workers in the region," he said.

"When this sort of thing happens, we think it's important that we support them, and make sure that they feel that they are well looked after and that they have support around them."

Manjimup is reliant on workers from the Pacific islands labour scheme. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Mr Cooper said the Manjimup team had organised the function to mark the passing of the men.

"We organised a little event to bring the Vanuatu community together to pay their respects and also to know there is a safe space they can come together and talk, and some of the other Palm workers came along to show their support," he said.

Manjimup-based farm worker Ricken Bininhi is from Vanuatu and said he had been saddened to hear of the deaths of the two men.

He maintained his support for the PALM scheme, saying the support provided in Australia allowed him to raise his family's standard of living.

"We in Vanuatu don't have more opportunities for making money; when we get here, we make our living in Vanuatu," he said.

The tragedy has also had an impact on the islander community on the east coast of Australia, in the regional community of Griffith in New South Wales, which has been a hub for farm workers from the Pacific Islands

Griffith-based community leader Wilkinson Royel said fundraising would take place this weekend to help the men's families.

The PALM scheme has come under scrutiny in recent years, in part because of the number of workers leaving their employers.

More news and current affairs from ABC Pacific From the international teams of ABC Radio Australia, ABC Australia, and ABC News, explore our comprehensive radio, digital, and video coverage of the Pacific all in one place.



In Victoria, the Australian Workers Union has also raised concerns over In Victoria, the Australian Workers Union has also raised concerns over the high rate of road deaths among PALM workers.

Manjimup Hotel co-owner Ed Fallens, who provides accommodation for many PALM workers, said he helped organise the function to help workers commemorate the men.

"With the amount they've given us as a community, I would have liked to have seen a community-wide dedicated service."

Investigations into the deaths are continuing, with anyone with information asked to contact WA Police on 131 444.

World.title: Driver in life-threatening condition after car rollover onto railway line
World.content:
One person is in a life-threatening condition after a serious crash on the Sunshine Coast this morning.

Police were called to a single-vehicle rollover at Nambour Connection Road in Kulangoor just before 8am.

The vehicle rolled onto a railway track, with the male driver suffering "critical injuries", according to the Queensland Police Service (QPS).

A Queensland Ambulance Service spokesperson said paramedics were on scene and assessing the driver.

Powerlines are also down near the site.

Police said diversions were in place, and they were turning around northbound traffic.

Nambour Connection Road northbound is closed just north of Oleander Drive.

"Disruptions to the rail network are expected for several hours while forensic examinations take place," QPS said.



All rail services between Palmwoods and Gympie North have been suspended, according to a Queensland Rail social media post.

"We are anticipating delays of up to 60 minutes on the Sunshine Coast line … Rail replacement buses have been organised," the post said.

More to come.

World.title: Vaccine program almost halves RSV hospitalisations of young babies
World.content:
A new immunisation program for pregnant mothers and newborns has almost halved the number of young babies being hospitalised with a serious respiratory virus, according to a new report.

The analysis, which compared 2024 hospitalisation data with 2025 numbers, showed a 43.8 per cent drop in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospital admissions across 13 hospitals Australia-wide in babies under three months old.

RSV, which is highly contagious and can cause pneumonia and bronchiolitis, is a leading cause of hospitalisation in infants aged under 12 months.

Approximately 12,000 Australian babies aged under one year old are hospitalised with RSV each year, mostly during the autumn and winter months.

Paediatrician Ushma Wadia (right) was the lead researcher on the RSV study. (Supplied: The Kids Research Institute Australia.)

Across the hospitals included in the study, the data also showed a 20.1 per cent reduction in hospital admissions of babies aged three to six months and 8.5 per cent for six to12-month-olds.

The preliminary results are undergoing peer review and the research was conducted by The Kids Research Institute Australia, the National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance and Monash University, in collaboration with 13 hospitals across Australia.

Pregnant women have had free access to the RSV vaccine under the National Immunisation Program since February last year.

Newborns who did not receive protection during their mothers' pregnancy were eligible for the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab through state and territory-funded programs.

Childhood vaccine coverage declines for fifth year in a row The latest immunisation data shows more than 80,000 Australian children aged five and under are not fully up to date with their vaccinations.

The report authors said the analysis showed babies born to mothers who had the vaccine were 80 per cent less likely to be admitted to hospital and babies who received the monoclonal antibody were 90 per cent less likely to be hospitalised.

Ushma Wadia, a paediatrician and clinician-scientist at The Kids Research Institute, said RSV was potentially deadly and could require treatment in intensive care units.

"If some babies are more severe, they may also need intubation or breathing support," said Dr Wadia, who is an investigator on unrelated studies funded by Pfizer and Sanofi, the companies that manufacture the maternal RSV vaccine and infant nirsevimab.

Pregnant women have been able to access free RSV vaccines under the National Immunisation Program since February 2025. (Reuters: Heiko Becker)

She said the immunisation program demonstrated "amazing" effectiveness over a single season.

" I'm very encouraged by these figures. I've seen that reduction on the wards, where we're not seeing these babies coming in with bronchiolitis as we did two years ago. "

Dr Wadia said RSV placed significant pressure on hospitals each respiratory season.

"Now we have the ability to… hopefully free up those beds that were being taken up by children that had RSV infection and ensuring that now we have beds and resources that are available for those who need them."

Vaccine a 'no-brainer' for first-time mum

Perth mother Katryna Cygler had the vaccine when she was pregnant with her first child, Hugo, who is now nine months old.

She said she was determined to protect her son.

"I had heard some pretty horrible stories from friends that had babies that had gone to hospital with the virus," Ms Cygler said.

"I just knew that it was a pretty deadly virus for some of the babies… so it was a no-brainer for me really to go ahead and have the vaccine."

Katryna Cygler wanted her son Hugo (pictured) to be protected. (Supplied: The Kids Research Institute Australia)

Paediatrician and clinical epidemiologist Terry Nolan, who was not part of the study, said the latest data was encouraging, but there needed to be a stronger focus on getting the vaccine to more pregnant women and the monoclonal antibody to more babies.

With full and effective delivery of the maternal and infant immunisation program, he said, "we could possibly even double those impact numbers down the track".

Professor Nolan said the government should adopt a target to have at least 95 per cent of infants protected, either through the maternal vaccine or the monoclonal antibody.

"That's a very simple thing to do," said Professor Nolan, who has received consultancy fees from Pfizer and Sanofi in the past.

What is RSV?

RSV is a highly infectious virus, spread via droplets, and is the most common cause of respiratory infections in children.

Most children will catch the virus at least once before they turn two, according to health authorities.

Symptoms include a runny nose, cough, fever, wheezing and difficulty breathing.

Co-author of the new study Nick Wood, a paediatrician and associate director at the National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance, said autumn marked the beginning of "RSV season" and numbers were already starting to rise.

"Every year around about now we see a rise in RSV cases before we see a rise in flu cases," he said.

Professor Wood, who is an investigator on an unrelated Sanofi sponsored vaccine trial, said it could be a terrible illness for babies and their parents.

"It's distressing and uncomfortable and worrying and anxiety provoking because having your baby lying in a bed connected to tubes, watching them struggle to breathe is quite distressing."

The maternal RSV vaccine is available to women between 28 to 36-weeks pregnant, to protect them and their child from the virus.

Nick Wood says RSV cases are already starting to rise this year. (Supplied: Nick Wood)

The baby gains some protection from the mother's antibodies and is less vulnerable in the first six months to severe disease.

In this week's federal budget, the federal government announced it would fund a free RSV vaccine for older Australians.

It will spend $449.3 million to list the vaccine Arexvy on the National Immunisation Program, making it free for patients over 75. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are eligible from the age of 60.

The study's "declaration of interest" reported several of the authors have worked on trials supported by pharmaceutical companies, including those that produce RSV vaccines and the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab, with no personal remuneration.

It also stated several had received travel and accommodation support or honorariums paid to their institutions for speaking and advisory roles.

World.title: Teenagers arrested during alleged arson attack on Melbourne CBD bar
World.content:
Police have arrested two teenagers who allegedly tried to set fire to a bar in Melbourne's CBD that has already been targeted by arsonists on multiple occasions.

Officers patrolling the area as part of Operation Eclipse spotted a white Kia wagon arrive outside Bar Bambi in ACDC Lane about 4:45am today.

Police said two males ran from the car carrying a jerry can, smashed a window at the bar and tried to pour fuel into the venue.

A discarded jerry can could be seen outside the venue on Friday morning. (ABC News: Stephanie Ferrier)

Officers moved in and arrested two 16-year-old boys but the driver of the vehicle fled the scene and could not be found.

It is believed to be the third time the bar has been targeted and the second time police have arrested people at the venue.

ACDC Lane has been the site of repeated arson attempts. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

'Terrifying' fires at suburban business

Police are also investigating an arson attack on a number of trucks at a business in Melbourne's inner-west overnight.

Victoria Police said two unknown offenders tried to set fire to a number of vehicles at the business in Tottenham about 1am.

One truck sustained moderate damage and nobody was injured in the incident.

Workers at a business in Tottenham extinguished fires that were set on a number of vehicles at a local business. (ABC News: Kate Meade)

The arsonists were interrupted by workers at the business, who then extinguished fires on several trucks.

One worker who did not want to be identified said the incident was "terrifying".

"Luckily we saw the fire and we immediately reacted on that one, and then we used a fire extinguisher to control the fire," he said.

"I think their intention was to burn all of the trucks, we have 15-20 trucks.

" Luckily we were here to react as quickly as we can, and then luckily they got, I mean strange to say luckily, but they were able to burn just five trucks. "

Several trucks were set fire in Sunshine North on Thursday night. (ABC News)

Police were unable to say if the incident was linked to a suspicious truck fire at Sunshine North earlier in the evening.

Two male offenders smashed the window of a truck in Cutts Street, Sunshine North, and set the vehicle alight.

They also attempted to set fire to another vehicle next to it but were unsuccessful.

Police said the offenders fled the scene in a white vehicle.

Anyone who witnessed either incident or has information has been urged to contact CrimeStoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Firefighters slam bureaucracy for slashing roadside burns by 90pc
World.content:
Country Fire Authority (CFA) firefighters claim they are being "hamstrung" by planned-burn bureaucracy, with approvals taking up to three years.

Firies have told the ABC there needs to be less red tape when it comes to burns on both council-controlled land and major arterial roadsides.

Barongarook CFA president Mike Evans said his family had been fighting fires in the south-west Victorian region for five generations.

Firefighters working on the Carlisle River bushfire in the Otways, early 2026. (Facebook: CFA South West)

Mr Evans said a procedural labyrinth had reduced the number of planned burns on private and council-controlled land by up to 90 per cent in the region over the past decade.

He said it came down to public pressure to stop planned burning.

"To put it bluntly it's arse-covering," Mr Evans said.

"We've seen our roadside burns, particularly in our forested communities … decrease to almost nothing.

Mike Evans says his family has been fighting fires for five generations. (Supplied: Mike Evans)

"We've been able to achieve very little with municipalities, particularly with the Colac Otway Shire, the roadsides and small blocks they own; we found it very difficult to get approval to do fuel management."

Colac Otway Shire Council has been contacted for comment.

Forest Fire Management Victoria (FFMVic) and the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) control burns on public land.

Local government councils, Rural Roads Victoria, and the Department of Transport are responsible for roadside fuel loads and have some control over private land burns.

Mr Evans said backburning was vital.

"I've had 40 years of experience … [planned burns] are not going to stop major wildfires, but they're going to lessen the impact of the fires in our community," he said.

Barongarook West CFA captain Steve Brookes said authorities needed to start thinking about burning even earlier in the year.

"Unfortunately, there's a lot of politics involved in burning," Mr Brookes said.

Steve Brookes says he is being "hamstrung by bureaucracy". (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

"The general public doesn't understand the need for it … and we need less politics and less influence by people who don't understand the real need.

" People just refuse to accept that burning is good for the environment, good for the ground, good for the vegetation. "

It comes after FFMVic exclusively revealed to the ABC how planned burns over the years in the Otway Ranges have definitively helped control recent bushfires.

But environmental groups believe the approach to planned burns needs a rethink.

Planned burns helped in Otways fires

In January, more than 15,000 hectares of land was burnt in the Otway Ranges bushfires.

Seventeen homes were razed and nearly 40 other structures damaged or destroyed.

New research from FFMVic has revealed a bushfire in Carslisle River burnt less intensely and less widespread in areas that had been sites of persistent planned burns over the past decade.

The areas include Tomahawk Creek, Timberjack Track, and Kennedy's Creek.

Spot fires that landed at a former burn site at Larsons Road self-extinguished.

Fire authorities say the Carlisle River blaze scorched right up into the canopy of trees in areas outside of planned burns (left), while areas in a planned burn (right) were not burnt as badly. (Supplied: DEECA)

Mr Evans said FFMVic made strategic fire breaks during the Otways bushfire, which cleared roadside undergrowth and ultimately gave CFA crews the chance to conduct vital backburning.

"That saved [our community]," he said.

Burns under scrutiny

The practice of planned burns has come under scrutiny in recent years, with some ecologists and scientists concerned that the research behind planned burning was thin.

Victorian National Parks Association campaigner Jordan Crook supported planned burns close to homes and other assets but said FFMVic's burns on large areas of public land did more harm than good.

"Intensely managing [land] 100 metres around assets is a better way to go about it rather than just burning out the back of the bush where no-one lives," Mr Crook said.

Jordan Crook says planned burning needs a rethink. (Supplied: Jordan Crook)

Mr Crook said he was concerned for native wildlife being more susceptible to predators such as feral cats and foxes if habitat was destroyed during backburning.

Otway Ranges Environment Network spokesperson Simon Birrell said the group was worried about the rate of fuel reduction burns in cool temperate rainforest areas.

"There's a bit of a grey line between where wet forest starts and ends, and whether they should be burning regularly or leaving the forests alone," Mr Birrell said.

Meanwhile, the Bureau of Meteorology has forecast a possible El Niño as early as May this year, increasing the chance Australia will face a warm and dry second half of 2026.

Large swathes of bushland was scorched in the Otway Ranges during the bushfires in January 2026. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

DEECA deputy chief fire officer and director of forest fire operations for Barwon Southwest Region, Scott Turner, said the organisation had a "really detailed program" for its planned burns.

The program involves multiple agencies, including the CFA and FFMVic, coming together to look at fire risk across the state.

Mr Turner said planned burns during the cooler months were carefully done to minimise fire risk without burning out the bush.

Scott Turner says Forest Fire Management Victoria's approach is backed by science. (Supplied: DEECA)

"It's not climbing up the trees and taking out the canopy," Mr Turner said.

"[The fires] are slow-moving and it's also allowing [wildlife] to get out of the way of the fire and also have pockets of habitat that remain."

He said planned burns were focused around townships and communities, while burning in remote locations prevented fuel from building up and potentially being set alight by embers thrown ahead or spot fires in extreme fire conditions.

"There's less likelihood that they will then become the next catastrophic and extreme fire event," Mr Turner said.

A Department of Transport and Planning spokesperson said roadside maintenance was prioritised based on risk.

"We work closely with relevant agencies, councils and emergency services to plan mowing and vegetation management programs and prioritise the highest-risk areas," the spokesperson said.

The CFA declined an interview.

In a statement, a spokesperson said it had exceeded its planned burn targets in the past two years but refused to say what these targets were.

World.title: Protesters say they are in chains at North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment
World.content:
Protesters of the controversial North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment say they have chained themselves to machinery at the site on Friday morning.

One of the protesters, named Hayley, told 891 ABC Adelaide that she chained herself to a gate on War Memorial Drive and that four others had chained themselves to machinery inside the golf course.

The ABC has contacted police, but is yet to confirm whether any arrests have been made this morning.

The course is undergoing a $45 million redevelopment, which has sparked significant protests while two people were arrested for trespassing on Thursday.

Police are also investigating a suspicious fire at the redevelopment site, hours after thousands protested at Parliament House on Wednesday night.

Police are treating a fire at the golf course from early Thursday morning as suspicious. (ABC News: Sophie Landau)

This morning, Hayley said police were at the site and she was prepared to be arrested "for a good cause".

Another protester Naomi, who was not taking part in the act but said she was part of the group protesting, said several people have chained themselves with padlocks at the golf course which would need to be cut by police officers.

"Absolutely people within our group are willing to get the arrest, fine, because they believe that it's absolutely worthwhile," she said.

"We are engaging in non-violence direct action … [we are] not being abusive, not doing anything that's violent."

Adelaide Park Lands Association president Mat Monti said his group did not organise the chaining but said this morning's act was "appropriate".

"As long as an action is peaceful and non-violent, we believe it is all appropriate to try and save these 585 trees," he said.

World.title: Why Millennials and gen Z feel ripped off by this budget
World.content:
Sweeping changes to investment tax breaks in Labor's new federal budget are supposed to appeal to Australians struggling to buy their first home, but the pitch is not landing with everyone.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the reforms would finally address intergenerational inequality, and likely hoped the defining image of his budget week would be his sunny social media reel chatting with young voters about the plan.

But within hours of the budget's release, satirical news site The Betoota Advocate had published a post skewering the government's tax changes.

Federal politics live updates: For the latest budget reactions and news from Parliament House, read our blog.

'Labor to finally even the playing field for younger Australians by stopping future generations from using the tax loopholes that boomers will be allowed to keep using,' it read.

The federal government's decision to grandfather negative gearing and Capital Gains Tax has renewed the narrative that young people are always disadvantaged, while existing home owners remain protected.

Budget 2026 winners and losers In the first full budget since Labor's landslide election victory last year, the government is putting some money back in workers' pockets and increasing taxes on investors. So who wins and who misses out?

On Wednesday, comedy duo Lachlan and Jaxon Fairbairn, better known as @fairbairnfilms, posted a skit on social media titled Buying a house in 2026. By the next day, it had received more than three-quarters of a million views.

"So everyone before me gets it good, and I get it shit," the video concluded.

Under Mr Chalmers' pre-budget reel on Instagram, one commenter posed a simple question — how is it fairer?

"Looks like you're just taxing us more and grandfathering the benefits for boomers," they wrote.

"This budget is a slap in the face to young people who are paying attention. AND WE ARE PAYING ATTENTION."

Why some Millennials and gen Z feel like they are losing

Most Millennials and gen Z won't be able to benefit from the generous system of tax breaks that many feel helped older generations get ahead.

Labor is planning to limit negative gearing to new builds and reduce the capital gains tax discount.

While these changes are designed to restructure how people make money in Australia (away from property investment), the measures are being grandfathered, which means people who already own property will hold on to most of their benefits.

Unless young people buy a newly built home, they will not get the same opportunity.

Online, there has been wide acknowledgement of the government's attempt to step toward a more equitable housing system.

Four charts that explain the story behind Labor's tax changes Just like it did in 2019, Labor is making an argument about wealth in Australia when it proposes negative gearing and capital gains tax changes.

But beyond those changes, supply remains the issue, and the people at the bottom of the property ladder continue to pay the highest price.

The budget projected the tax changes would help 75,000 homes change hands from investors to first home buyers, and slow property price rises by two per cent.

Macquarie Business School's David Orsmond said that figure was a drop in the ocean.

"That two per cent is relative to a growing price trend that has seen house prices grow by 400 per cent in the last 25 years, double the growth of wages," he said.

"It's a step in the right direction, but it's not going to make a substantive difference to their ability to acquire a home at an acceptable price."

The tax changes are expected to cut housing supply by 35,000 homes, as weaker investor demand reduces the pace of new construction.

As a counter, the government is spending $2 billion over four years for councils and utility companies to build roads, pipes, power and sewage connections to speed up the construction of new housing, which will increase supply by 65,000 homes.

That means the net impact of the budget policies is 30,000 extra homes.

The number of new homes under construction has already been steadily rising since a collapse after the pandemic.

The politics of grandfathering

The government's decision to grandfather negative gearing is as much about politics as economics.

In part, it was used to avoid a sudden sell-off of properties from investors worried about losing benefits overnight.

There was also a risk that failing to grandfather would significantly drive up rents as investors scrambled to cover their losses.

But it was also a political calculation by Labor. Australians bought investment properties under the existing system and, in some cases, built long-term retirement plans around those tax settings.

Suddenly changing the settings would have exposed the government to accusations that it was punishing people who simply played by the rules of the day.

Albanese and Chalmers take political gamble Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers have made generational equity the test for this budget.

These changes are also a backflip on the promises Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made during last year's election campaign, when he categorically ruled out changes to negative gearing or the CGT discount.

No-one has predicted when the negative gearing of existing properties will fully exit the housing market.

Over time, many investment properties naturally shift from negative to positive gearing as rental income increases and debt levels fall, although the timeline can vary significantly depending on the market and loan structure.

That can also happen when an investor hits retirement and chooses to sell their property or pay off the mortgage.

Gen Z will now have to rethink money

A growing cohort still pursuing the housing dream has turned to investing in shares and ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds) to build wealth.

One of the benefits for young people is that they can get started with only a small amount of money.

Although the government has touted changes to CGT as a measure targeted at people who invest in housing, it will also capture other assets, including shares.

That means people who buy new shares, crypto, or other investments will pay more tax when they sell those assets, regardless of their income.

The CGT changes are also grandfathered, so gains made before the new rules come into effect is taxed at the discounted rate.

With house prices expected to steadily rise in Australia, investment in housing is still likely to turn a profit, but that will depend more on continued demand for homes rather than a good deal on tax concessions.

The challenge now for the government is how to communicate this change to a generation of people who already feel like they are being left behind.

World.title: Melanie Lynskey joins the fight for justice after NZ's Pike River Mine disaster
World.content:
At around 3.44pm on November 19, 2010, the first of several devastating methane explosions tore through the Pike River Mine, north-east of Greymouth on Aotearoa's South Island.

Twenty-nine men were killed in one of the country's worst industrial disasters.

They included Anna Osborne's husband, Milton, and Sonya Rockhouse's 21-year-old son, Ben. His brother, Daniel, was one of only two survivors to walk free from the tunnel.

More than 15 years later, Osborne and Rockhouse are still campaigning for stronger workplace safety laws, recognition of corporate manslaughter and the return of their loved ones.

"We've had no truth, no justice and no accountability, so we're going to keep going until we do," a stoic Rockhouse tells ABC Arts.

"There's a whole part of the grieving process that we still have to have," Osborne adds.

"It's devastating to me that I can't bury my husband."

Resilience and love

The powerful new film Pike River, directed by Robert Sarkies, dramatises their battle.

Yellow Jackets lead Melanie Lynskey portrays Osborne, with Mystery Road: Origin star Robyn Malcolm as Rockhouse.

Anna Osborne (Melanie Lynskey) and Sonya Rockhouse (Robyn Malcolm) have fought for 15 years to bring justice to the men they lost in the disaster. (Supplied: Matt Grace / Madman Entertainment)

Sarkies brought Fiona Samuel's screenplay to Lynskey.

"Rob used to be my boyfriend," Lynskey reveals over a video call from the beautiful home she shares with husband Jason Ritter in Los Angeles.

"Not for long, luckily for him, as it was a very tumultuous time in my life. But he was such a sweet person, very kind-hearted and so very talented. I've always held a special place in my heart for him."

Lynskey, who made her big screen debut opposite Kate Winslet in Peter Jackson's Heavenly Creatures and appeared alongside Cate Blanchett and Rose Byrne in Mrs America, didn't take much convincing.

"It's a story of resilience and frustration, of friendship and deep love, managing to survive after the worst thing imaginable happens," Lynskey says.

"That these two women found and leaned on each other felt so profound to me."

It was no small task, stepping into their shoes.

"Gosh, I felt a huge responsibility," Lynskey says.

" It's a such a big part of New Zealand's history that's affected so many people's lives. I just wanted to get it right and do them justice. "

Lynskey heaped pressure on herself.

"It's a tough thing for me, as a perfectionist, riding the line between trying to approximate an actual human being, then you have to be an actor, with dialogue written for you that's not exactly how it happened."

Loading Instagram content

That, and the small matter of her adopted American persona.

"Honestly, I was a bit worried about my accent, because it's all over the place," Lynskey laughs.

"Luckily, spending time with Anna, I was able to get an intonation without doing a full-on impression, because she made it very clear she didn't want that."

Osborne and Rockhouse embraced the actors on set.

"It was actually incredible," Lynskey recalls.

"I kept thinking, 'How would I feel in this situation?' But they were just so loving, so excited for us to do it and so supportive, very emotional and willing to tell their story. Understanding their dynamic was just so useful for me and Robyn."

Having admired Malcolm from afar, "for as long as I can remember," the reality did not disappoint.

"It was the easiest job of my life, becoming best friends with Robyn," Lynskey says.

"She's such a force of nature, so present, grounded and truthful and surprising in every moment. It was a dream. I genuinely love her."

So much so, they got matching tattoos.

"Anna and Sonya bonded in court over sharing a bag of lollies," Lynskey says.

"In the movie, they gave us Liquorice Allsorts. Anna and Sonya were like, 'We hate them'.

"Robyn and I were like, 'We actually do too'. I don't know if anyone likes them, but that's what we got tattooed and they look really cute."

The good fight

The real women's bond was invaluable during Pike River's location shoot near the disaster site.

"It was dragging up 15 years of the past, and that was extremely difficult for both Sonya and I, at times, because the raw emotion came flooding back," Osborne says. "But we trusted Rob."

The four women, pictured here at the film premiere in New Zealand, forged a tight bond. (Supplied: Rebecca McMillan)

A few expletives were loosed when Sarkies told Rockhouse he'd cast Malcolm.

"I said, 'She can't play me. She's gorgeous. She's Cheryl West from Outrageous Fortune'. I just could not see it, but Robyn did a fantastic job. So many of my friends have said 'She got you down to a tee'."

Osborne was similarly impressed.

"Melanie's such a beautiful soul. I may have been a bit more boisterous, but she did a wonderful job. Robyn and I are incredibly blessed to have two amazing women playing us."

Both agree Pike River has boosted their long and hard-fought campaign.

"We were showing the movie in Dunedin, down the bottom of the South Island, and an older man came up to me and said, 'I've always thought that you and Anna need to get on with it and move on'," Rockhouse recalls.

"I thought, 'Oh gosh, here we go,' but then he said, 'Now I've seen the movie, I've completely changed my mind. I'm 100 per cent behind you, keep going and don't give up'.

"And that made me so happy, because he's only one person, but he'll go on and talk to somebody else, and so on and so on."

The families of the disaster have still not been able to bury their men, who remain entombed in the mine, which was sealed shut. (Supplied: Matt Grace / Madman Entertainment)

That word of mouth is invaluable.

"We don't want our loved ones to have died in vain," Osborne says.

" They should have been protected. But instead, the company put profit over safety. Losing a loved one in the workplace is a nightmare. "

They never want anyone to find themselves in their position.

"There's so much at stake," Osborne says.

"For the people of New Zealand and Australia, going to work each day, it's a goddamn right that they return home to their loved ones each night."

While Osborne and Rockhouse insist they are "ordinary women", Lynskey doesn't see it that way.

"They're the most extraordinary women," she insists.

"They have fought for so many years to make their voices heard. The tragic part of the whole story is that it's unresolved. But they're still fighting.

"I hope Pike River brings a little bit more awareness."

Pike River is in Australian cinemas from May 14.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Declining WA year 12 results prompt new calls for release of overdue review; Perth icon Boffins Books to close down
World.content:
After more than 37 years a Perth CBD staple – Boffins Books – is closing down, citing the rise in work from home culture as one of the key reasons they were forced to shut down.

Boffins Books in the Perth CBD has been forced to close down. Boffins Books/ Facebook

“Since we first opened in 1989, our mission has been to provide facts at your fingertips,” a press release from the shop stated.

World.title: Trump China visit LIVE: President agrees with Xi that US was a ‘declining nation’, blames Biden, ahead of discussions on Iran, trade and Taiwan
World.content:
China has agreed to buy 200 Boeing aircraft, Trump told the Fox News Channel, far fewer than analysts had expected, and the plane maker’s shares fell.

Details of the deal were not immediately available, including when and which types of jets would be delivered, but the number was much lower than the roughly 500-plane package that sources had told Reuters was under discussion ahead of yesterday’s meeting between the two leaders.

Boeing has a lot riding on the success of its latest generation 737 airliners. AP

“One thing he agreed to today, he’s going to order 200 jets ... 200 big ones,” Trump said on Fox News’ Hannity, referring to Xi.

Boeing shares fell 4.1 per cent during market trading on Thursday, US time. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wall Street’s reaction to the announcement.

World.title: The miracle, mid-air kick that stunned the reigning premiers
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The miracle, mid-air kick that stunned the reigning premiers Peter Ryan Updated May 15, 2026 — 8:41am ,first published 12:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Cats will never disappear. All the prayers, predictions and prognostications from opposition supporters have amounted to nothing. Shaun Mannagh celebrates one of his five majors for the night. Getty Images They are still there, nagging away like the lawn you haven’t mowed, the tail-light you haven’t fixed, or the dirty clothes staring back at you from the washing basket. Their demolition of the reigning premiers by 41 points at the Gabba on Thursday night, just five days after smashing Collingwood, could be described as a statement, or a brutal reminder, or simply the perfect execution of a well-planned mission.



The club that has played in preliminary finals in eight of the past 10 seasons, and three of the past six grand finals, will be sniffing at the flag again. That’s the only conclusion that can be reached after their Thursday night throttling of the Lions. Bailey Smith and Tanner Bruhn were again influential for Geelong. AFL Photos Cats coach Chris Scott was content with the performance, but knows nothing memorable is won in May. “There is still a lot of footy to be played, but we are confident we will get better,” Scott said.



The Cats’ midfield is supposed to be a weakness but no one worth listening to has got that message through to them yet, except Port Adelaide, anyway. The combination led by young ruckman Mitch Edwards is workmanlike on paper, with rock star Bailey Smith surrounded by bass players in Tom Atkins, Tanner Bruhn, Shaun Mannagh and tagger Oisin Mullin. View post on X Star runner Max Holmes sits in defence to be called upon when needed, while Patrick Dangerfield just marches into the centre if an old and occasionally wise head is needed. Mullin kept dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale quiet, while Hugh McCluggage could not have his normal influence. Will Ashcroft was reasonable, but when Geelong dialled the volume up early in the third quarter none of those stars could be heard over the din as the Cats’ lead stretched to 42 points.



The Cats lost the clearance count but scored 31 more points from clearance than their opposition as they have made that a strength in the past six weeks. Jeremy Cameron kicked three goals for the Cats to take his season tally so far to 27. AFL Photos Mannagh, who was in a rut (a dirty word in some parts) six weeks ago when he described his game against the Hawks on Easter Monday as “a shocker”, has bounced back with a vengeance. He was superb in the second half, kicking three goals in a three-minute-and-50-second burst that was perhaps the most exciting sub-four-minute stretch since Roger Bannister ran his famous mile. OK, that might be an exaggeration, but it was a great watch, nonetheless, with two of his goals coming from kicks out of mid-air. The Lions, with their dwindling supply of small defenders, had no answer. View post on X



One important swing from the grand final was that the Cats had Tom Stewart back in the team, while the Lions were without the injured Dayne Zorko. Stewart, who missed last year’s decider through concussion, intercepted marks and returned anything the Lions could fire inside 50 with interest. He was outstanding. He is commanding a defence that is desperate to keep their foot on their opponents’ throats, while the forward line is predictably unpredictable, with Jeremy Cameron and Shannon Neale the constants inside 50 as the game’s best coach feeds players through the forward half, with Jack Henry making a cameo as he returned from injury. Cameron kicked three to take his season tally to 27, the same number he had after round 10 last year. He finished with 88 goals in 2025. Chris Fagan and his Lions have some thinking to do. Getty Images The Lions will be in contention, too, with their coach Chris Fagan suggesting their hunger for the contest wasn’t as it had been recently with three six-day breaks in a row a potential factor. Justifiably, he said there was no need to “hit the panic button”. Fagan would be well aware the Lions had only lost once to the Cats in their previous five encounters heading into the match. “Well done Geelong. They were great,” he said. The reality is the Cats have been great with monotonous regularity over the past 20 years – their smarts and hard work still the benchmark for most clubs in the competition. They play another team with the same reputation, Sydney, next week at home in a game that will either elevate Geelong’s standing, or confirm the reality they live by, which is that every opponent is tough.



The most ominous comment came from Bailey Smith post-game when he spoke to Channel Seven after another excellent 34-disposal performance. “We don’t want to peak just yet,” Smith said. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street climbs; Boeing falls as China plane order disappoints
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street climbs; Boeing falls as China plane order disappoints Stan Choe Updated May 15, 2026 — 8:36am ,first published 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rose to more records Thursday after Cisco Systems joined the parade of US companies reporting fatter profits for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. The S&P 500 climbed 0.8 per cent to set an all-time high for a second straight day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 370 points, or 0.7 per cent, and finished above the 50,000 level for the first time since the war with Iran began, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.9 per cent to its own record. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.31am AEST pointing to a gain of 46 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.1 per cent on Thursday to break a four-session losing streak. The Australian dollar was weaker at US72.19¢.
